Daniel is treating “Darwinian process” as a second, independent arrow of time alongside thermodynamic entropy, but that independence is the hidden assumption. A Darwinian process (replication + heredity + variation + differential survival) is itself a way of *amplifying* small differences into macroscopic regularities, yet it only runs in environments that supply free energy and allow waste heat—i.e., open systems far from equilibrium. That puts it closer to the family of “dissipative structures” than a rival to entropy’s arrow: selection builds local order by exporting disorder, not by escaping the thermodynamic bookkeeping ([Prigogine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilya_Prigogine); Schrödinger’s classic framing in [*What is Life?*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_Is_Life%3F)). If the post’s intent is “Darwinism is time-asymmetric even though microphysics is mostly time-symmetric,” then the missing bridge is boundary conditions: selection looks irreversible largely because it exploits persistent records (genomes, balance sheets, institutional memory) that are easy to create in a low-entropy past and hard to “uncreate” without fantastically fine-tuned conditions.

That matters for the “Von Neumann economy” claim too. Growth isn’t an intrinsic preference of “the economy” so much as a property of a replication-like dynamic under constraints: firms and strategies that reinvest and copy tend to occupy more market share *conditional on* energy, resources, and institutions that make expansion feasible. The slogan “if a thing makes more of itself, we are gonna see more of it” compresses Darwinism into tautology and quietly drops key requirements (competition for limited resources; heritable variation; and a selection environment). Daniel may be gesturing at “universal Darwinism” in the sense of generalized replicator dynamics ([Dennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Dennett)), but without those ingredients it becomes hard to distinguish “Darwinian” from mere positive feedback.

On “Darwinian process in reverse time”: the strict time-reversal of a selection trajectory would look like lineages *systematically un-copying* successful adaptations and reconstituting diversity from homogenized populations—possible in principle only if the system is conditioned on an extraordinarily special future boundary (the analogue of reversing a movie of diffusion). We don’t observe such dynamics for the same reason we don’t see spontaneous un-mixing: not because laws forbid them, but because the required macrostate constraints are astronomically improbable. If Daniel wants insight into causality, the promising angle is that selection produces *apparent* causal stories (“this trait caused success”) by filtering histories, but that explanatory asymmetry still rides on the deeper asymmetry in what information can be stably recorded and propagated in time.
